chief_complaint: dull upper stomach pain and feeling bloated after eating greasy food
hpi_details: 23-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of dull right upper quadrant abdominal pain and bloating that typically occur 30 to 60 minutes after consuming fatty meals. The episodes last for a few hours before gradually subsiding. Denies fever, chills, or jaundice.
ideas: He thinks he has bad indigestion or food poisoning triggered by grease from fast food he eats after late shifts.
concerns: He is worried that an attack will strike while he is on duty at work or that it could be his appendix about to burst.
expectations: He hopes to have an ultrasound of his abdomen and walk away with medication to settle his stomach after meals.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Biliary Colic is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes ordering an abdominal ultrasound, advising a low-fat diet, and consulting general surgery, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: dull upper stomach pain and feeling bloated after eating greasy food
Key HPI features: 23M presents with recurrent dull RUQ pain and bloating 30-60 minutes after fatty meals, lasting a few hours before resolving. No fever or jaundice.
Objective/Exam findings: Vitals stable, afebrile. Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness in the right upper quadrant. Negative Murphy's sign.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Biliary Colic.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute cholecystitis without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Fever or pain that doesn't settle after several hours — would suggest cholecystitis.
management_principles: Order right upper quadrant abdominal ultrasound to identify gallstones.
Advise a strict low-fat diet to prevent further symptomatic episodes.
Refer for elective outpatient general surgery consultation for consideration of cholecystectomy.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) Clinical Guidelines

reference_soap.subjective: 23-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of dull right upper quadrant abdominal pain and bloating that typically occur 30 to 60 minutes after consuming fatty meals. The episodes last for a few hours before gradually subsiding. Denies fever, chills, or jaundice.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 76, BP 120/80, Temp 37.0C, SpO2 99%. Abdomen: Soft, non-distended. Mild tenderness to deep palpation in the right upper quadrant. Negative Murphy's sign. No rebound or guarding. No scleral icterus or jaundice.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Order RUQ abdominal ultrasound to confirm cholelithiasis. 2. Educate patient on a strict low-fat diet. 3. Refer to general surgery for elective cholecystectomy evaluation. 4. Return precautions for fever, intractable vomiting, or unremitting pain.

learning_objectives: Recognize the classic presentation of Biliary Colic (postprandial RUQ pain, absence of fever/jaundice).
Differentiate Biliary Colic from Acute Cholecystitis using history and physical exam findings (e.g., Murphy's sign).
Implement an evidence-based management plan including ultrasound, dietary modification, and surgical referral.

teaching.one_liner: A gallstone temporarily blocks the gallbladder outlet after fatty food, causing dull right-upper-quadrant pain and bloating that eventually settles.
red_flags: Fever or pain that doesn't settle after several hours — would suggest cholecystitis

must_ask.say: Does the pain come on after eating fatty food?
Do you feel bloated or overly full along with the pain?
Does the pain spread to your shoulder blade?
Have you had any fevers or chills?
Have you noticed any yellowing of your skin or eyes?
Has anyone told you before that you have gallstones?

history.answer: I've been having this dull upper stomach pain and feeling really bloated whenever I eat greasy food.
It feels like a dull, heavy ache combined with tight bloating and fullness.
It's mainly in my upper right abdomen, right under the rib cage on that side.
Sometimes the dull ache spreads around toward my right flank and up into my right shoulder blade.
The attacks started about a month ago. Each episode begins roughly thirty to sixty minutes after eating and lasts two to four hours before gradually fading.
It definitely acts up after fatty or oily meals, like fried chicken, pork belly, or cheeseburgers.
If I eat late at night, the ache keeps me awake for a few hours, but it doesn't wake me from sleep on an empty stomach.
No, I don't get a burning sensation behind my breastbone or sour fluid coming up into my throat.
I get bloated after eating, but I can finish a regular meal without feeling full after only a couple of bites.
No, swallowing food and drinks is completely normal and painless.
I feel nauseated during the peak of the discomfort, but I haven't thrown up.
My appetite is normal, though I try to steer clear of fried foods now, and my weight has stayed the same.
No, I haven't thrown up blood, and my bowel movements are normal brown with no black or tarry stools.
No, I haven't had any lightheadedness, dizziness, or unusual exhaustion.
No, walking, climbing stairs, or exercising doesn't trigger or worsen the pain.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or night sweats at all.
No, my skin and eyes look completely normal, and my urine hasn't turned dark.
I've never been told I have gallstones, and I have never had an ultrasound done on my belly.
I don't take aspirin or anti-inflammatory drugs like ibuprofen. I tried acetaminophen once, but it didn't make much difference.
I eat fried or heavy foods a few times a week and have one cup of coffee daily, but my stress levels are manageable.
No, I've never had an upper endoscopy or any testing or treatment for stomach bacteria.
I thought it was just really bad indigestion or mild food poisoning from eating too much greasy fast food on late shifts.
I'm worried this might be my appendix getting ready to burst, or that an attack will hit during my new job's probationary period and cost me my shift.
I don't have any chronic medical illnesses like high blood pressure, diabetes, or liver problems.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I'm not currently taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or nutritional supplements.
No, I don't have any allergies to medications or foods.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used electronic cigarettes.
I only drink socially, having one or two beers maybe a couple of times a month.
I'm a university student living in a rented studio near my campus.
My mother had her gallbladder removed due to gallstones, but nobody in my family has stomach cancer or liver disease.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 120/80 mmHg, pulse 76 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 37.0 C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Well-developed young male appearing comfortable at rest with no acute distress.
Conjunctivae are pink without pallor, and sclerae are clear without icterus or jaundice.
No palpable left supraclavicular lymphadenopathy or cervical lymph node enlargement.
Abdomen is flat and non-distended with no surgical scars or visible pulsations.
Normoactive bowel sounds heard across all four quadrants with no vascular bruits.
Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness on deep palpation in the right upper quadrant, with no palpable mass.
No rebound tenderness or involuntary abdominal wall guarding.
Negative Murphy's sign with no sharp arrest of inspiration on deep palpation beneath the right costal margin.
